label: Decision owner and sign-off
title: The documents refer to a decision point (“{anchor}”), but no one is named as the final decision owner
why: Unowned decisions stall work and get re-opened late. Naming the owner early is the cheapest risk reduction.
question: Who has the final say on “{anchor}”, and how are disagreements escalated?
nextStep: Name one decision owner per major decision.
disproof: A named approver, RACI or escalation path for “{anchor}”.

label: Success criteria
title: The project goal is stated (“{anchor}”), but no measurable success criteria are written down
why: Without agreed criteria, finishing becomes a matter of opinion.
question: How will we know the “{anchor}” has succeeded, in numbers?
disproof: A KPI, acceptance criterion or definition of done for the “{anchor}”.

justifications.irreversibility: Work wasted on the wrong target

label: Dependency tracking
title: The plan relies on a “{anchor}”, but no owner or lead time is recorded
why: External dependencies are outside your control and are the most common cause of silent delay.
question: Who owns the “{anchor}” and what is its committed date?
nextStep: List each dependency with an owner, date and fallback.
disproof: A dependency register or committed date for the “{anchor}”.

label: Stakeholder communication
title: Several groups are affected (“{anchor}”), but no communication plan is described
why: Surprises damage trust faster than bad news does.
question: Who needs to hear what, how often, regarding the “{anchor}”?
disproof: A communication plan or reporting cadence.

label: Contingency / buffer
title: A fixed date or amount is set (“{anchor}”), but no contingency or buffer is included
why: Plans without slack turn every small delay into a missed commitment.
question: How much contingency is built into the “{anchor}”, and who can release it?
nextStep: Add explicit buffer to the schedule and budget.
disproof: A contingency, buffer or float allowance for the “{anchor}”.
